C005.subject: remote work
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: remote work individual task productivity]

[PATH:empirical] Controlled field experiment comparing individual task completion times and error rates for collaborative tasks in co-located vs. remote settings — Directly tests the causal claim by measuring productivity differences under controlled conditions, isolating the effect of remote work on interdependent tasks.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal analysis of digital collaboration logs (e.g., Slack, Trello) from a large organization, tracking task completion speed and rework rates before and after a shift to remote work — Provides real-world evidence on how loss of informal coordination and rapid feedback loops affects individual productivity in collaborative tasks over time.

[PATH:theoretical] Review of media richness theory and coordination costs literature (e.g., Daft & Lengel, 1986; Malone & Crowston, 1994) applied to remote work contexts — Explains the mechanisms behind the hypothesis, offering a framework to predict when and why remote work decreases individual productivity in interdependent tasks, and guiding empirical tests.

scope.domain: individual performance metrics for collaborative, interdependent tasks

qualifier.evidence: loss of informal coordination and rapid feedback loops

C006.subject: remote work
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: remote work individual task productivity]

[PATH:empirical] A randomized controlled trial comparing task completion rates and output quality between in-office and remote workers under controlled task conditions, with independent performance metrics. — Direct causal evidence on individual productivity differences can be isolated by controlling for task type, time allocation, and managerial oversight.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of longitudinal field studies on remote work productivity, focusing on individual-level output (e.g., lines of code, customer service tickets resolved) from corporate datasets. — Aggregating existing empirical studies can reveal whether the hypothesized decrease holds across contexts or is moderated by factors like task complexity or self-discipline.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical modeling of attention allocation and procrastination in distributed work environments, incorporating variables like social presence and feedback delay. — A formal model can specify conditions under which loss of oversight leads to productivity decline, generating testable predictions for empirical validation.

qualifier.evidence: loss of real-time managerial oversight and informal collaboration leads to procrastination and reduced output

C007.subject: asynchronous communication tools in remote work
C007.object: cross-functional idea generation when structured ideation protocols are used
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: asynchronous communication tools in remote work cross-functional idea generation when structured ideation protocols are used]

[PATH:empirical] Controlled experiment comparing cross-functional teams using asynchronous tools (e.g., Slack, Miro) with vs. without structured ideation protocols (e.g., brainwriting, SCAMPER) on idea novelty and count metrics. — Directly tests the causal claim by isolating the effect of structured protocols in asynchronous settings, addressing the disputed status with high internal validity.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal field study in global remote organizations (e.g., GitLab, Zapier) analyzing archival communication data (e.g., thread depth, cross-department mentions) against innovation output (e.g., implemented ideas) under varying levels of ideation structure. — Provides ecological validity and temporal scope (2020-2024) to observe whether structured protocols moderate the relationship between asynchronous tools and cross-functional idea generation in real-world settings.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing literature on computer-mediated communication and team creativity, focusing on moderator effects of protocol structure (e.g., nominal group technique vs. free brainstorming) in asynchronous contexts. — Synthesizes prior findings to identify whether the effect is consistent across studies, helping resolve the disputed status by quantifying overall evidence strength and boundary conditions.

C008.subject: remote work
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: remote work collaboration and innovation outcomes]

[PATH:empirical] A longitudinal field experiment comparing team-level innovation metrics (e.g., patent filings, product iterations) across matched hybrid, fully remote, and co-located teams in knowledge-economy firms (e.g., tech, R&D) post-2020. — Direct causal evidence from controlled settings can isolate the effect of remote work on collaboration and innovation outcomes, addressing the disputed status.

[PATH:literature] Systematic meta-analysis of peer-reviewed studies (2021-2025) on remote work and team creativity, focusing on moderators such as task interdependence, digital tool usage, and synchronous/asynchronous communication frequency. — Synthesizing existing evidence will clarify whether the hypothesis holds across contexts and identify boundary conditions, given the moderate confidence and global scope.

[PATH:theoretical] Agent-based simulation modeling of knowledge-sharing networks under varying degrees of remote interaction, calibrated with empirical data from distributed teams. — Theoretical models can test mechanisms (e.g., weak ties, serendipity loss) that explain or refute the hypothesized enhancement, especially for team-level creative output in the post-pandemic era.

qualifier.geographic: global, with emphasis on knowledge-economy regions
